guides.title: Resolve a session before checking roles
guides.summary: Use application-owned session validation to populate the trusted request user, then apply role or permission middleware.
guides.markdown:
Authentication resolves a trusted user from a session. Authorization decides which operations that user can perform. createAuth accepts extractSessionId, validateSessionId and resolveUserById callbacks. The application owns session storage, expiry, revocation and user lookup. Use an opaque session token and trusted server storage. A claimed user ID, role or permission from the browser is not authentication.

Run auth.middleware before authorization guards. It populates context.get('user') after session and user validation. Missing or invalid sessions stay anonymous. Provider failures also stay anonymous. createAuthorizer builds middleware around application hasRole and hasPermission callbacks. Missing callbacks deny the corresponding checks. requireRole accepts any listed role. requireAllRoles requires every listed role. Anonymous denials use 401 and authenticated permission denials use 403 by default.

Install the middleware in the framework application or relevant page/layout guards. Transport guards use the transport request. Apply resource authorization per action for record access. A WebSocket connection guard does not recheck each later message. Native entrypoints must parse and authorize explicitly.

createLoginHandler accepts credential validation and an application session creator. The provider can also supply createSession for reuse. Set cookie attributes and merge returned headers into the actual response. Define logout, expiry and session rotation in the application. OAuth setup requires provider credentials and callback handling. This example does not create a login route or issue a cookie.

The package currently ships TypeScript source through its main entry. Use the framework Vite pipeline or a compatible TypeScript loader. File presence and static signatures do not prove execution in plain Node. The executable example uses fixed in-memory session fixtures to test middleware ordering and role decisions. These fixture tokens are not production credentials or a persistent session implementation.

guides.title: Authorize a specific server record
guides.summary: Define typed actions against trusted user and record data. Keep permission presentation separate from server enforcement.
guides.markdown:
createResourcePolicy<Resource, User>() accepts named boolean decision callbacks. It retains the action names and application types. Policies read the user from trusted server request context. The application supplies record lookup and persistence. Browser state and resource IDs remain untrusted input.

Use can for a boolean decision and authorize to enforce access. authorize returns the accepted record or throws ResourceAuthorizationError. Anonymous denials have COSSACK_AUTH_UNAUTHENTICATED and status 401. Authenticated denials have COSSACK_AUTH_FORBIDDEN and status 403. Missing records are denied. Callback exceptions are internal failures, not deliberate denials.

permissions returns frozen booleans for presentation. Recheck authorization on the server before mutation even when the UI hides a button. policy.action adapts parsed input and trusted request context to Server authorization metadata. Attach it through @Server({ input: schema, authorize: policy.action(...) }). The lookup receives the owned AbortSignal. Do not derive its actor or tenant from browser fields.

policy.middleware performs request-specific lookup and authorization before an HTTP handler. Direct native method calls do not run RPC metadata. Parse input and call authorize explicitly at native entrypoints. Authorization is a decision at one time. Use a transaction or conditional write that repeats trusted ownership predicates when a record can change.

Pass the signal to lookup I/O and check cancellation before effects. Aborting stops waiting for a policy callback but cannot terminate work that ignores cancellation. Rule maps are fixed after construction. Unknown actions and nonboolean decisions do not authorize access.

The executable example uses local Hono request contexts and fixture records. It proves decisions, frozen presentation permissions and parsed-input action lookup. It does not authenticate a real user, make a network request or write to a database. Run it with the framework pipeline or a compatible TypeScript loader because this package ships source.

guides.title: Handle OAuth failures by code and stage
guides.summary: Use fixed library diagnostics for configuration, state, provider and application mapping failures without exposing callback or credential data.
guides.markdown:
createOAuth supplies signed state and PKCE for cookie-based authorization flows. Use a request-scoped secret resolver when server bindings exist only on the request context. The application owns provider credentials, local account mapping and session creation.

OAuthError exposes code, stage, status and an optional numeric providerStatus. Messages are fixed library text. Errors retain no raw exception, provider response body, authorization code, token or credential. toJSON returns only this diagnostic data. Configuration failures throw synchronously when the kit or route is constructed. Redirect preparation failures use the default diagnostic response.

Callback onError receives an immutable OAuthError. Return a Response to control the failure response. Returning nothing preserves the default response. A throwing onError produces COSSACK_OAUTH_ERROR_HANDLER_FAILED. Log error.toJSON rather than the callback URL, cookie, tokens or request context. Context still contains application request data.

Invalid callback parameters or state produce status 400. Denied consent produces 403. Provider rejection, token exchange and user-info failures produce 502. Configuration, redirect preparation, account mapping and error-handler failures produce 500. Account mapping includes the application onUser callback and any session creation it performs. Failures do not undo application writes or sessions already created.

Configured cookie-based callback handlers clear their matching state cookie on success and failure, including denied consent and missing parameters. Cookie deletion is browser cleanup, not an atomic server-side replay store. Provider authorization codes must still be single-use. The application owns stronger replay, session expiry and rotation guarantees. Stateless mode requires application CSRF protection and does not use the state cookie or PKCE verifier.

The example invokes only denied and malformed callbacks. It uses fixture configuration and does not contact a provider, exchange a code or create a session. TypeScript source needs a compatible loader or bundler.
